Title: Quantifying the Impact of Job Placement and Routing on Network Efficiency in AI Clusters

Abstract
High-performance computing (HPC) clusters are essential for train-
ing large-scale AI models, yet they often suffer from severe under-
utilization due to network bottlenecks. This paper investigates the
critical role of job placement in multi-tenant AI clusters and its
impact on network performance. We propose a flow-level system
model that jointly considers job placement, network topology, and
routing strategy to evaluate link loads and congestion. By analyzing
optimal, random and state-of-the-art placement strategies across
modern network topologies, we demonstrate that placement deci-
sions significantly influence network efficiency. Our results show
that job placement cannot be ignored even under optimal routing,
and that existing placement strategies are dependent on the rout-
ing strategy. This work underscores the importance of prioritizing
job placement, as suboptimal placements can lead to significant
performance degradation in AI workloads on HPC infrastructure.

resources, especially for data-intensive workloads. This is illustrated

This inefficiency is primarily attributed to memory and network
that cannot saturate the employed computer resources, leading to
suboptimal performance.
Distributed Machine Learning (DML) workloads, in particular,
are highly susceptible to network bottlenecks [25]. These work-
loads involve extensive data exchanges between nodes, especially
during the stages of gradient aggregation and parameter updates
in distributed training. The high volume and frequency of these
communications can easily overwhelm the network infrastructure,
resulting in significant delays and reduced overall efficiency.
The challenge of network bottlenecks in HPC clusters is com-
plex, and is often mitigated by introducing optimized topologies
[1, 10, 15–17], routing strategies [12, 22], and flow control [19, 20,
31]. A significant portion of research is dedicated to addressing
these aspects to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of HPC
interconnects and systems. The aforementioned mitigations aim to
minimize network congestion based on a given demand of flows.
However, even with optimal routing and flow control, achieving
an unsaturated network can be infeasible due to poor locality. A
more effective approach prioritizes optimizing flow demand as a
direct outcome of job placement first, followed by targeted con-
gestion mitigation. Since flow demand inherently stems from job

placement decisions, addressing it at the source is essential for
alleviating network bottlenecks.
This paper delves into the intricacies of job placement within
multi-tenant HPC clusters, emphasizing the interaction between
job placement and the underlying network stack. By exploring
the impact of various placement strategies in combination with
topologies and routing strategies, we aim to provide insights into
optimizing HPC environments for AI workloads, thereby unlocking
their full potential. The main contributions of this work are the
following:
• Develop a flow-level system model for evaluating workload,
placement, topology, and routing.
• Evaluate optimal placement against state-of-the-art place-
ment strategies.
• Quantify and compare the impact of job placement and rout-
ing simultaneously.
2
Related work
Over the years, extensive research has been conducted on job place-
ment, typically in the form of analytical studies or proposed method-
ologies. Most of this research focuses on either resource allocation
or task mapping. In resource allocation, the objective is to select a
set of compute nodes on which a pending job will be executed. In
task mapping, the goal is to assign the job’s individual processes to
the previously allocated compute nodes. In both cases, the overar-
ching aim is to optimize a performance metric that affects either
job efficiency or overall system performance.
Traditionally, resource management has primarily focused on
computational resources, often neglecting the network infrastruc-
ture and its associated resources. However, recent work has demon-
strated that incorporating network awareness can improve per-
formance. For example, several strategies have been proposed to
manage network resources, either directly or indirectly. Techniques
such as LaaS [27] and Jigsaw [23] reduce inter-job interference
in fat-tree topologies by isolating network usage, achieving up
to 40% reductions in job turnaround time. For Dragonfly topolo-
gies, the Level-Spread allocation policy [30] exploits the topology’s
hierarchy to distribute jobs and balance load. Beyond topology-
specific methods, more general-purpose techniques have been de-
veloped to support arbitrary network topologies. One such method
is TreeMatch, introduced by Georgiou [7], a topology-aware job
mapping technique designed for tree-based network topologies.
TreeMatch leverages network affinity and communication patterns
to guide the mapping process using graph partitioning techniques.
Building on this, Jeannot proposed TopoMatch [13], which extends
the approach support for arbitrary, non-tree topologies. A comple-
mentary placement strategy, LibTopoMap [11] employs a heuristic
based on graph similarity to identify efficient mappings, further re-
fining them through congestion prediction models. Both approaches
fundamentally rely on optimization techniques rooted in shortest-
path calculations and hop-bytes metrics. However, this reliance
limits their effectiveness in systems that employ adaptive routing-
–crucial for modern, low-diameter network topologies–because
such topologies offer limited path diversity, reducing the benefits
of shortest-path-based optimizations.
Research [3, 8, 21, 29] consistently highlights that "poor" place-
ment can severely degrade both application and system perfor-
mance. However, there is no understanding of what constitutes
"poor" placement beyond linear or random placement.
In low-diameter topologies, random job placement is often en-
couraged, as it allows arbitrary traffic patterns to approximate
uniform traffic behavior–under which these topologies are known
to achieve high throughput [4, 14]. However, Jokanovic [14] demon-
strated that, for certain adversarial traffic patterns on dragonfly
topologies, random placement alone is insufficient. In this work,
we extend this analysis to a broader range of topologies and to
traffic patterns characteristic of AI workloads. Furthermore, we
show that while random placement tends to perform poorly on
average, it nonetheless possesses the potential to yield near-optimal
placements under specific conditions.
3
Flow-level system model
We employ a flow-level network model to investigate the impact of
job placement under various routing strategies. The model takes as
input the workload, job placement, network topology, and routing
strategy. Based on these inputs, it evaluates the resulting network
behavior and quantifies performance implications. A schematic
overview is provided in Figure 1.
In a multi-tenant system, multiple independent jobs execute
concurrently. Our analysis begins with this set of jobs. The job’s
workload is represented by a set of static flows, where each flow
denotes a volume of data transferred from process 𝑝𝑖to process
𝑝𝑗. These flows are captured in a demand matrix 𝐷𝑤, where each
non-zero element 𝑑𝑤,𝑖𝑗corresponds to the communication demand
from 𝑝𝑖to 𝑝𝑗. The overall system demand is represented by a block-
diagonal matrix, where each block 𝐷𝑤corresponds to the demand
matrix of job 𝑤.
Unlike the traditional approach—which perform job placement
sequentially in two distinct steps: (1) allocating available compute
endpoints, and (2) mapping processes to the allocated endpoints—
our method performs joint allocation and mapping across all jobs
simultaneously. Job placement can be viewed as a mapping func-
tion from processes to compute endpoints. Assuming an equal
number of processes and endpoints, the set of all possible place-
ments corresponds to the set of all permutations of the processes.
In our matrix-based formulation, this implies that a job placement
is represented by a permutation of the demand matrix 𝐷.
The network topology is modeled as a graph 𝐺(𝑉, 𝐸), where 𝑉
represents the set of network switches, and 𝐸the set of all links
between them. We abstract away the compute endpoints, as con-
gestion is more likely to occur in the network core (i.e., switch-to-
switch links) than in the switch-to-endpoint connections. To isolate
core network effects, we assume that all endpoints connected to a
given switch are allocated exclusively to a single job. Given a job
placement– and its associated permutation, the permutated demand
matrix is then linearly mapped onto the topology, assigning each
process 𝑝𝑖to the compute units connects to a single switch 𝑣𝑖.
Finally, according to the selected routing strategy, we distribute
the flows across the network links and compute the resulting link
loads. These link loads form the basis for evaluating the combined
effects of workload, placement, topology, and routing.

3.1
Workloads
The most common way to parallelize machine learning workloads
is through data parallelism. In this paradigm, the model is repli-
cated across all compute units, and the dataset is divided into mini-
batches. Each unit independently performs forward and backward
passes. To maintain a consistent model across all units, a synchro-
nization phases is required during which gradients computed by
each unit are exchanged. This gradient exchange can be imple-
mented using various communication patterns, such as rings, trees,
or meshes, and can follow either in a centralized (parameter-server)
or decentralized (allReduce) communication model [26]. In this
work, we base our workloads on the analysis by Zerwas [28], who
studied the communication patterns of three state-of-art distributed
ML frameworks.
• Duplex Broadcast: A single root process 𝑝0 communicates
uniformly and bidirectionally with all other processes 𝑝𝑖.
Non-root processes do not communicate with each other.
This pattern reflects the typical parameter server training
approach.
• Ring: Processes are arranged in a ring topology. Process
𝑝𝑖communicates uniformly and bidirectionally with its 2
neighbors 𝑝𝑖−1 and 𝑝𝑖+1.
• All-to-All: Every process 𝑝𝑖communicates with all other
processes. Corresponds to clique-based gradient exchange
and generalizes to tree and star topologies, although the flow
volumes may vary.
For larger models, additional forms of parallelism, such as pipeline
and operator parallelism, can be employed. To model the communi-
cation patterns arising from these strategies, we follow the descrip-
tions provided by Hoefler [10].
• Torus: Processes communicate in a 3D torus. Every process
𝑝𝑖,𝑗,𝑘communicates uniformly and bidirectionally with its 2
neighbors 𝑝𝑖,𝑗−1,𝑘and 𝑝𝑖,𝑗+1,𝑘in each of the three dimensions.
Each dimension corresponds to one of the three paralleliza-
tion approaches: data, pipeline, or operator parallelism. By
selecting only one or two dimensions, this model can be
reduced to a 1D (ring) or 2D torus.
Figure 2 provides an overview of the topologies and correspond-
ing demand matrices for each workload type.
3.2
Placements
In addition to basic placement strategies such as linear and random
placement, we also consider several advanced methods proposed

for arbitrary network topologies (see Section 2), including Topo-
Match [13] and LibTopoMap using Reverse Cuthill McKee (RCM)
algorithm [11].
3.3
Topologies
We consider three promising low-diameter network topologies
Dragonfly [15], Polarfly [16], and Polarstar [17]. These topologies
outperform traditional tree-based architectures by offering low
latency and cost-effective high bandwidth, thanks to their minimal
diameter.
However, this advantage comes at the cost of limited shortest-
path diversity–often, only a single shortest path exists between
node pairs. Consequently, static routing strategies frequently fall
short in effectively balancing network traffic. To overcome this limi-
tation, adaptive routing becomes essential, dynamically distributing
traffic based on real-time network conditions and utilizing non-
minimal paths to avoid congestion. Yet, this adaptability introduces
additional complexity, making it more difficult to predict actual
network load. In such topologies, it is therefore critical to integrate
routing strategies into job placement decisions, as routing behavior
plays a significant role in determining overall system performance.
3.4
Routing
In this work, we consider two routing strategies: static routing
and optimal routing. Our static routing strategy is based on Equal
Cost Multi Path (ECMP) routing, where traffic is evenly distributed
across all available shortest paths between source and destination
nodes.
For optimal routing, we adopt a global load-balancing strategy
that aims at minimizing network congestion by a specific perfor-
mance metric. We formulate this as a maximum concurrent flow
problem, expressed as a linear program:

To reduce the complexity of the linear program, we leverage the

allows us to limit the size of 𝑃𝑖𝑗without significantly compromising
performance.
We use maximum link load as our primary network perfor-
mance metric, as it correlates strongly with both latency and overall
throughput [5, 18]. This is particularly important in distributed ma-
chine learning (DML), where tail latency–the delay experienced by
the slowest communication–directly impacts job completion times
due to frequent synchronization barriers and has direct impact on
job completion times [6, 25]. By minimizing the maximum link
load, we aim to reduce worst-case latency and improve training
efficiency.
4
Results
4.1
Optimal Placement
If we want to analyze the impact of job placement, we can start of
by examining the theoretical optimal placement by iteration over all
possible placements. Given that the number of possible placements
grows factorially, exhaustive evaluation quickly becomes infeasible-
–even for small systems. However, thanks to symmetries available
in most traffic patterns (and network topologies), we can reduce
the search space to the set of non-isomorphic placements.
Figure 3 presents the maximum link loads for all non-isomorphic
placements on a 13-node Polarfly topology, for both static and opti-
mal placement. The workload is generated by randomly selecting
job sizes until the system is full. For each job we used the All-to-All
workload type and randomly selected an intensity factor to scale
the demand.
By comparing the mean of maximum link load for both routing
strategies, we can quantify the benefit of optimal routing: it achieves
a 1.96x reduction in maximum link load compared to static routing.
Similarly, analyzing the reduction in maximum link load between
the optimal placement and the average placement allows us to as-
sess the impact of optimal placement. Under static routing, optimal
placement reduces the maximum link load by a factor of 1.44, while
under optimal routing, this factor is 1.11. These results indicate
that while optimal routing reduces the sensitivity to placement, the
benefits of optimal placement remains significant. Notably, the im-
pact of switching from static to optimal routing (1.96x) exceeds the
impact of optimal placement under static routing (1.44x), indicating
the continued importance of adaptive routing strategies.
Additionally, the performance of various placement strategies is
shown, revealing a strong dependence on the underlying routing
strategy. For the traffic pattern considered here, TopoMatch per-
forms best under optimal routing, whereas under static routing, the
other placement strategies yield better results.

4.2
Random Placement
As topology size increases, computing the optimal job placement
becomes infeasible, limiting its practicality to small systems. To
assess routing and placement strategies at scale, we adopt a ran-
domized sampling approach. By evaluating random placements, we
analyze the mean and variability of maximum link loads. This ex-
periment targets topologies with over 100 routers, offering insights
into large-scale behavior.
For each topology and each workload class we consider 200
global workloads. These workloads are generated using the same
methodology as in the optimal placement analysis. For each global
workload we evaluate 200 random placements both under static
and optimal routing.
Figure 4 illustrates the distribution of the reduction in maximum
link load achieved by optimal routing compared to static routing. As
expected, optimal routing consistently outperforms static routing,
as indicated by all reduction values being greater than one. Notably,
the benefits of optimal routing are more pronounced for Polarfly
and Polarstar, particularly under ring and torus workloads. This ob-
servation aligns with findings from Besta et al. [2], which highlight
that Dragonfly topologies inherently offer greater shortest-path di-
versity, thereby reducing the relative advantage of adaptive routing.
Moreover, the wide spread observed in these distributions suggests
that these configurations are highly sensitive to job placement, un-
derscoring the importance of intelligent placement strategies in
achieving consistent performance.
To assess the impact of placement, we once again examine the
reduction in maximum link load between the optimal placement
and the average placement. Unlike the earlier experiment involving
a truly optimal placement, the "optimal" placement in this context
refers to the best placement found out of the set of 200 randomly

We observe a similar trend as in the optimal routing experi-
ments: the reduction in maximum link load is generally lower
when optimal routing is applied. Nevertheless, for some config-
urations the reduction remains notable, indicating that optimal
placement still provides meaningful benefits even under adaptive
routing. Interestingly, for torus and ring traffic on Dragonfly, the
load reduction is even greater under optimal routing. This some-
what counterintuitive result can again be attributed to Dragonfly’s
higher shortest-path diversity.
When comparing the impact of placement versus routing, it is
evident that routing has the greater influence. In nearly all config-
urations, the improvement achieved by switching from static to
optimal routing exceeds the improvement gained by selecting the
best versus average placement. However, it is important to note that
our analysis is based on a set of only sampled 200 placements, and
that optimal routing is often infeasible in practice due to its com-
putational complexity and system constraints. Meaning that our
analysis overestimates the load balancing capacity commonly used
routing strategies. Therefore, we can conclude that while routing
plays a dominant role, the impact of placement remains significant
and cannot be overlooked in practical scenarios.
Rather than focusing solely on the benefits of selecting the best
random placement, it is equally important to understand the detri-
mental impact of selecting a suboptimal (or "poor") placement. In
Figure 6, we illustrate the reduction in link load achieved by the
5-shot random placement against that of the single-shot placement.
In the 𝑛-shot random placement approach, we randomly sample 𝑛
candidate placements and use our flow-level system model to select
the most effective one.
When compared with Figure 5, it becomes evident that, on aver-
age, the benefit of best placement yields greater performance than
the 5-shot random placement. However, the long tails in the distri-
butions indicate that the 5-shot placement method is already highly
effective at avoiding poor single-shot placements–sometimes even
outperforming optimal routing in terms of load balancing.
These findings are consistent with the observations of Jokanovic
[14], who showed that random placement alone is insufficient for
managing adversarial traffic patterns in Dragonfly topologies. Sim-
ilarly, our results demonstrate that single-shot random placement
is inadequate for traffic patterns of AI workloads.
5
Conclusion
This work has demonstrated that job placement plays a critical role
in determining network efficiency in HPC-clusters, particularly for
AI workloads. Through a comprehensive flow-level system model,
we jointly analyzed the effects of job placement, network topology,
and routing strategy on maximum link utilization. Our results show
that while optimal routing significantly improves network per-
formance, it does not eliminate the impact of placement decisions.
Even under adaptive routing, poor placement can lead to substantial
performance degradation. Conversely, random placement–though
commonly used–proves insufficient for complex AI traffic patterns,
especially in low-diameter topologies with limited path diversity.
We further demonstrated that the simple yet effective 𝑛-shot ran-
dom placement strategy significantly mitigates the risk of poor
placement outcomes.
Future research should focus on developing scalable methods
that make random placement strategies more network-aware, and
incorporating real-time network conditions to enhance placement
evaluation.

Abstract: High-performance computing (HPC) clusters are essential for train- ing large-scale AI models, yet they often suffer from severe under- utilization due to network bottlenecks. This paper investigates the critical role of job placement in multi-tenant AI clusters and its impact on network performance. We propose a flow-level system model that jointly considers job placement, network topology, and routing strategy to evaluate link loads and congestion. By analyzing optimal, random and state-of-the-art placement strategies across modern network topologies, we demonstrate that placement deci- sions significantly influence network efficiency. Our results show that job placement cannot be ignored even under optimal routing, and that existing placement strategies are dependent on the rout- ing strategy. This work underscores the importance of prioritizing job placement, as suboptimal placements can lead to significant performance degradation in AI workloads on HPC infrastructure.
